lessons.title: The earth, rocks and weathering
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Geography — Physical geography (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Name the layers of the earth
Describe igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks with examples
Distinguish weathering from erosion and name the types of weathering
reviewNotes: Cameroon examples of rock types (e.g. volcanic basalt of the western highlands) are only mentioned in general terms; a teacher should check local examples against the syllabus.
Syllabus references and scope to be checked against the official GCE Board syllabus; all facts, names and figures to be verified by a geography teacher before release.

blocks.md: The earth has four main layers. The **crust** is the thin, solid outer skin on which we live. Under it lies the **mantle**, a thick layer of very hot rock that can flow very slowly. Below the mantle is the **outer core**, which is liquid, and at the centre the **inner core**, which is solid.

blocks.caption: Layers of the earth (not to scale)
blocks.alt: Concentric circles showing crust, mantle, outer core and inner core.

blocks.title: Three families of rock
blocks.md:
- **Igneous rocks** form when molten rock (magma or lava) cools and hardens. Granite cooled slowly underground; basalt cooled quickly at the surface.
- **Sedimentary rocks** form from layers of sand, mud or shells pressed together over time. Examples: sandstone, shale, limestone.
- **Metamorphic rocks** are old rocks changed by great heat and pressure. Examples: marble (from limestone) and slate (from shale).

**Weathering** is the breaking down of rock **in place**, by the weather, plants and chemicals. **Erosion** is the wearing away and carrying of material by rivers, waves, wind or ice. In weathering nothing is transported; in erosion there is movement.

blocks.title: Types of weathering
blocks.md:
- **Physical (mechanical):** rocks crack when heated by day and cooled at night; outer layers may peel off like the skin of an onion (exfoliation).
- **Chemical:** rainwater is slightly acid and dissolves some rocks, especially limestone (carbonation). In hot, wet regions chemical weathering is very fast and produces deep red soils.
- **Biological:** roots grow into cracks and widen them.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Weathering is not erosion: weathering happens without transport.
- Basalt and granite are both igneous; do not call granite 'metamorphic'.
- Chemical weathering is fastest where it is both hot and wet, such as the equatorial region of southern Cameroon.

blocks.title: Example 1: classify rocks
blocks.statement: A student finds a rock made of layers of sand grains in a river bank near Bamenda. Which family does it belong to and why?
steps: Layers of sand grains pressed together point to deposition of sediments.
Rocks made of compacted sediments are sedimentary.
The probable rock is sandstone.

blocks.title: Example 2: identify the weathering
blocks.statement: On a hot day a rock face in the Far North reaches a very high temperature; at night it cools quickly and flakes appear. Name the process.
steps: Large daily temperature changes make the outer rock expand and contract.
No chemicals or plants are involved, so it is physical weathering.
Flaking in layers is called exfoliation.

lessons.title: Rivers: course and landforms
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Geography — Physical geography (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Define source, tributary, confluence, mouth and watershed
Describe the work of a river in its upper, middle and lower courses
Name the main river landforms and explain how a meander and an ox-bow lake form
reviewNotes: Names of Cameroonian rivers and their destination (Benue to the Niger; Sanaga, Wouri, Nyong to the Atlantic) to be verified on a map by a teacher.
Syllabus references and scope to be checked against the official GCE Board syllabus; all facts, names and figures to be verified by a geography teacher before release.

blocks.md: A river begins at its **source**, often in highlands. **Tributaries** join it and the meeting point is a **confluence**. The river ends at its **mouth**, where it enters a sea or lake. The high ground that separates two river basins is the **watershed**. Water drains from a watershed into the **river basin**.

blocks.caption: Long profile of a river (schematic)
blocks.alt: A sloping line shows the river falling from its source through three courses to its mouth.

blocks.title: Upper, middle and lower course
blocks.md:
- **Upper course:** steep, fast, mainly vertical erosion. Features: V-shaped valleys, rapids, waterfalls, interlocking spurs.
- **Middle course:** gentler slope; the river swings from side to side and forms **meanders**.
- **Lower course:** flat land; much deposition. Features: wide floodplain, levees, ox-bow lakes, delta or estuary.

**Waterfalls** form where a layer of hard rock lies over softer rock: the soft rock is worn away faster and the water plunges over the edge. A **meander** is a bend: erosion is strongest on the outside, deposition on the inside. When a loop is cut off at a narrow neck, it becomes an **ox-bow lake**.

blocks.title: Estuary and delta
blocks.md:
- An **estuary** is the wide, tidal mouth of a river where fresh water meets the sea; the Wouri estuary near Douala is an example.
- A **delta** is a fan of deposited sediment built at the mouth when the river drops more material than the sea removes.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- Do not say that a river erodes only in the upper course: it erodes in every course, but the type and place of erosion change.
- A tributary joins the main river; a distributary leaves it (as in a delta).
- The Benue flows north to join the Niger in Nigeria, but the Sanaga and the Wouri flow to the Atlantic.

blocks.title: Example 1: name the feature
blocks.statement: Water falls over a hard layer of rock and a deep plunge pool lies below. In which course is this feature most likely, and how did it form?
steps: A waterfall needs a steep gradient, which is typical of the upper course.
Hard rock lies over softer rock; the soft rock is eroded faster.
The overhang collapses and the waterfall retreats upstream.
blocks.answer: A waterfall in the upper course, formed by differential erosion.

blocks.title: Example 2: sequence of an ox-bow lake
blocks.statement: Put in order: A) the neck is cut by a flood, B) the meander grows larger, C) the loop is sealed by deposition and becomes a lake, D) erosion on the outside bend and deposition inside.
steps: The process starts with erosion and deposition on a bend (D).
The meander then grows larger and the neck narrows (B).
A flood cuts through the neck (A) and the cut-off loop is sealed (C).

lessons.title: Coasts: erosion and deposition
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Geography — Physical geography (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe how waves erode and deposit
Explain how cliffs, caves, arches and stacks form
Explain longshore drift and the formation of beaches and spits
reviewNotes: Teacher to verify the Limbe black-sand statement and whether local coastal case studies are required by the syllabus.
Syllabus references and scope to be checked against the official GCE Board syllabus; all facts, names and figures to be verified by a geography teacher before release.

blocks.md: Waves are caused by wind blowing over the sea. **Destructive waves** are steep and strong, and they erode the coast. **Constructive waves** are low and gentle; they push material up the beach and build it. Waves erode by **hydraulic action** (force of water and trapped air), **abrasion** (hurling stones), **attrition** (stones wearing each other) and **solution** (dissolving).

blocks.caption: A cliff and wave-cut platform
blocks.alt: A cliff with a wave-cut platform at its base on a sea coast.

blocks.title: From cliff to stack
blocks.md:
1. Waves attack the base of a cliff and cut a notch.
2. The notch grows into a cave.
3. A cave cut through a headland becomes an arch.
4. The roof of the arch collapses, leaving a stack.
5. The stack is worn down to a stump.
The cliff retreats and leaves a flat **wave-cut platform**.

Deposition builds beaches of sand and pebbles. Waves often hit the shore at an angle: the swash carries material up the beach at that angle, and the backwash pulls it straight down. Little by little the material moves along the coast. This is **longshore drift**.

blocks.title: Spit
blocks.md: A **spit** is a long ridge of sand or shingle joined to the land at one end and stretching into the sea or across a river mouth. It forms where the coast changes direction and longshore drift carries material beyond the bend.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- Erosion forms cliffs, caves, arches and stacks; deposition forms beaches and spits. Do not mix them up.
- Mangrove swamps along the Cameroon coast protect the shore and are a habitat for fish; they are sheltered, muddy coasts rather than rocky cliffs.
- Beaches near Limbe have dark sand because it comes from volcanic rock.

blocks.title: Example 1: sequence
blocks.statement: Arrange the stages: stack, arch, cave, wave-cut notch.
steps: Waves first cut a notch at the base.
The notch becomes a cave, then a cave cut through a headland is an arch.
The arch roof collapses leaving a stack.

blocks.title: Example 2: longshore drift
blocks.statement: Waves arrive from the south-west at an angle to a beach running north-south. In which direction is material moved overall?
steps: Swash carries material up the beach in the direction of the waves, towards the north-east.
Backwash pulls it back at right angles, so it is carried a little further along each time.
The overall movement follows the angle of the incoming waves along the coast.
blocks.answer: Material moves along the beach in the general direction the waves are travelling (northwards).

lessons.title: Volcanoes, earthquakes and plate movements
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Geography — Physical geography (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe the earth's plates and the three types of plate boundary
Describe the parts of a volcano and the main types of eruption product
Explain the causes and effects of earthquakes
Link these ideas to Mount Cameroon and the Cameroon Volcanic Line
reviewNotes: Mount Cameroon height (about 4,000 m), its location near Buea, 'highest in West and Central Africa' and the 1986 Nyos event are to be verified. The explanation of the Cameroon Volcanic Line is deliberately general.
Syllabus references and scope to be checked against the official GCE Board syllabus; all facts, names and figures to be verified by a geography teacher before release.

blocks.md: The crust is broken into large pieces called **plates**. They move very slowly (a few centimetres a year) because of heat currents in the mantle. Most volcanoes, earthquakes and fold mountains occur near the plate boundaries.

blocks.caption: Cross-section of a volcano (schematic)
blocks.alt: A cone-shaped volcano with a vent, crater, lava flow and magma chamber.

blocks.title: Plate boundaries
blocks.md:
- **Constructive (divergent):** plates move apart; magma rises and makes new crust (mid-ocean ridges, rift valleys).
- **Destructive (convergent):** plates move together; one may sink under the other, producing volcanoes, earthquakes, ocean trenches or fold mountains.
- **Conservative (transform):** plates slide past each other; earthquakes are common, volcanoes are not.

A **volcano** is an opening where magma reaches the surface. Magma rises through a **vent** to the **crater**. Eruptions throw out lava, ash, gas and volcanic bombs. A volcano is **active** if it has erupted in recent history, **dormant** if it is quiet but may erupt again, and **extinct** if it is not expected to erupt.

An **earthquake** is a shaking of the ground caused by a sudden release of energy as rocks move along a break called a **fault**. The point underground where it starts is the **focus**; the point directly above it on the surface is the **epicentre**. Earthquakes are recorded by a **seismograph** and their strength is given as a magnitude.

blocks.title: Cameroon
blocks.md: Mount Cameroon, near Buea, is an active volcano and the highest mountain in West and Central Africa; it has erupted several times in recent decades. It belongs to the **Cameroon Volcanic Line** of mountains and crater lakes that runs from the coast towards the north-east. Lake Nyos is a crater lake where a deadly release of gas occurred in 1986.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Do not confuse the focus (underground) with the epicentre (on the surface).
- Volcanoes are not found only at plate boundaries (there are hotspots), but most are.
- Fold mountains form where plates push together, not where they move apart.

blocks.title: Example 1: identify the boundary
blocks.statement: Two plates are moving towards each other and one is being pushed under the other. A line of volcanoes and a deep ocean trench lie along the boundary. Which type of boundary is this?
steps: The plates move towards each other, so it is not constructive or conservative.
One plate sinks (subduction) and melts, feeding volcanoes.
Therefore it is a destructive boundary.

blocks.title: Example 2: focus and epicentre
blocks.statement: An earthquake begins 10 km below the ground. A town stands directly above that point. Which word describes the town's location, and which word describes the point 10 km below?
steps: The point below the ground where the earthquake starts is the focus.
The point on the surface directly above the focus is the epicentre.
The town is at the epicentre, so it will probably feel the strongest shaking.
